newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Mass protests enjoy Balkan revival.
newsitem.headline: Mass protests enjoy Balkan revival.

text.p: Albania's opposition on Wednesday called for anti-government protests, joining a Balkan revival of the mass protests that removed communist governments across eastern Europe.

As Yugoslav protests entered day 59 and Bulgarian rallies arrived at day 10, hundreds of Albanians took to the streets of Tirana blaming the government for the collapse of a get-rich-quick pyramid scheme.
Albania's opposition Socialist Party called for mass demonstrations to protest at an economic crisis it claims was created by the ruling Democratic Party.
"We want our money back. (President) Sali Berisha, you are a thief. (Prime Minister Aleksander) Meksi, you are a thief. Down with the dictatorship," the crowd chanted.

In Yugoslavia, where protests against cancellation of local election results by the ruling Socialists are in their ninth week, the Zajedno opposition coalition comes up with ever more inventive themes to persuade supporters to turn out day after day in freezing temperatures.

In Bulgaria, where an economic crisis has fuelled calls for general elections, opposition leaders admit they were inspired by nightly television pictures from Belgrade and protesters have adopted some of their tactics, particularly the deafening use of whistles, hooters and metal dustbin lids.
On Wednesday, protesters threw household rubbish at the parliament building.

Albania's ruling Democrats are staunchly anti-communist and enjoyed the backing of the West until they were accused of fixing general elections last year, while the governments of Serbia and Bulgaria are successors to former communist regimes.
Serbian communists, home-grown rather than imposed by Moscow, have ruled without interruption in Belgrade since 1945, surviving the revolutions in eastern Europe intact.
Police in all three countries, no longer tools of the communist state and frequently badly paid, often privately sympathise with the protesters.

Zajedno last week called for a "Talk to Cops" campaign to win security forces over to their cause. Demonstrators celebrating Orthodox Christmas gave out Christmas kisses -- on cheeks or the visors of riot helmets.

Many of the police surrounding the Albanian demonstrators were definitely on their side. "It's a big problem for us too because about three quarters of police have put their money in pyramid schemes," said a high-ranking police official.
Even the riot police hopping up and down to keep warm outside the Bulgarian parliament on Wednesday took up one of the opposition's chants: "Whoever isn't jumping is a cop".

Bulgaria is a conservative society with an elderly population and little tradition of violent mass protest, but voters who elected the Socialists in December 1994 have lost patience with their inability to halt economic collapse.

Bulgarian newspapers described Sunday's rally in Sofia as the biggest since 1990, when tens of thousands turned out to protest at the continuation of communist rule by senior colleagues of ousted leader Todor Zhivkov.

"The people in the streets are not just supporters of a party or a coalition but a nation that has been betrayed," said Bulgarian President Zhelyu Zhelev, an outspoken critic of the ruling Socialists.
